opus-5.5.text:
I think the key thing to understand is that pretraining alone gives you a model that knows a lot, but it doesn't really give you a model that knows how to *act* over a long horizon. When you pretrain on internet text, you're learning to predict the next token. That's a very local objective. Even with instruction tuning or SFT on demonstrations, you're mostly imitating short, clean trajectories, and the model never really experiences the consequences of its own mistakes.

Operator is doing tasks in a browser, things like booking something, filling out forms, navigating across several pages. These tasks might take dozens of steps. And the real difficulty is not any single step; it's that errors compound. If you click the wrong button at step five, you need to notice that at step seven and recover. Imitation learning is notoriously bad at this, because in the demonstration data the expert never makes that mistake, so the model has never seen what recovery looks like. This is the classic distribution-shift problem we've known about in robotics and RL for a long time.

Reinforcement learning changes that, because the model is trained on its own rollouts. It explores, it fails, it gets a reward signal, usually just whether the task was ultimately completed, and it has to figure out which of its behaviors led to success. Through that process you start to see emergent behaviors that nobody explicitly taught: the model checks whether a page actually loaded, it backtracks when something looks wrong, it breaks a task into subgoals. In a sense the long-term planning is not designed in; it emerges because it's what gets rewarded.

I'd connect this to what we saw with reasoning models like o1. The chain-of-thought there is essentially a long-horizon trajectory in thought space, and RL is what taught the model to reflect, to say "wait, this is wrong," and to try another path. Operator is a similar idea, but the trajectory extends into an actual environment with real state changes. So I see it as the same recipe, a strong pretrained prior plus large-scale RL with outcome-based rewards, applied to agentic settings.

That said, I don't want to overclaim. There are still big challenges. Reward is sparse, so credit assignment over long horizons is hard. Building environments that are diverse, realistic, and verifiable is a huge engineering effort; honestly I think environment and infrastructure work is often the real bottleneck, more than the algorithm. And the models are still somewhat brittle when they leave the training distribution. But directionally, I'm quite convinced that RL is the essential ingredient. Without it you get a model that can describe a plan. With it you start to get a model that can actually carry one out, and adjust when reality doesn't go according to plan.

r001.rationale: The response describes emergent behaviors and notes that models remain brittle outside the training distribution, but it does not clearly characterize RL as eliciting the foundation model’s generalization ability on sufficiently complex tasks.

r002.rationale: After describing demonstration-based SFT, the response says RL trains the model on its own rollouts, where it explores, fails, and learns from rewards.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts demonstrations that omit mistakes with RL-trained recovery, and says the model learns to notice errors, backtrack, and try another path.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key thing to understand about Operator is that long-term planning isn't something you can get purely from imitation. If you only do supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations of people browsing the web, the model learns to mimic individual actions, but it doesn't really learn why those actions matter for the final goal. Every step it takes is a little bit off, and over a trajectory of fifty or a hundred steps those errors compound. The agent drifts, clicks the wrong thing, and then has no idea how to recover, because the demonstration data never showed it being in that weird state.

Reinforcement learning changes the objective. Instead of "predict the next action a human took," the objective becomes "did you actually complete the task." The reward is tied to the outcome, so credit gets assigned backward across the whole trajectory. The model is pushed to care about whether an early decision, like which search query to use or whether to open a new tab, makes the later steps easier or harder. That's essentially what planning is: making current choices in service of a future state.

There are a few things that fall out of this. First, exploration. During RL the agent tries things that aren't in any human dataset, including making mistakes, and it learns recovery behaviors because recovering gets rewarded. That robustness is something I don't think you can distill from demonstrations alone. Second, the model learns to allocate effort. With outcome-based reward it starts to figure out when to slow down and verify, say, check that the right date is selected before clicking confirm, and when it's fine to move fast. Third, you get a kind of implicit decomposition. A long task gets broken into subgoals not because anyone labeled them, but because that structure is what reliably gets the reward.

I'd also say the reasoning-model lineage matters here. The same recipe that made the o-series models good at long chains of thought, which is RL on verifiable outcomes, transfers to agentic settings. Thinking for a long time about a math problem and acting for a long time in a browser are, structurally, the same problem: you have many sequential decisions, sparse feedback, and you need to learn which intermediate steps actually lead somewhere.

The hard parts are on the environment and reward side. Web tasks are noisy, websites change, and defining a clean success signal for "book me a reasonable flight" is genuinely difficult. So in practice a lot of the engineering effort goes into building environments and reward models that are reliable enough for RL to work, rather than into the algorithm itself. My view is that whoever builds the best environments and reward signals will get the best planning ability, and the RL algorithm is comparatively the easy part.

r001.rationale: The response describes RL improving long-term planning and robustness on extended tasks, but does not clearly characterize its role as eliciting the foundation model’s generalization ability.

r002.rationale: It says RL lets the agent try actions absent from human datasets, describing exploration beyond the demonstrations discussed earlier.

r003.rationale: It says the agent learns recovery behaviors through RL, which clearly communicates self-correction after the demonstration-based behavior described earlier.

astra-6.text:
I think reinforcement learning plays a very important role, because operating a computer is fundamentally a sequential decision-making problem. You don’t just need to take one correct action. You need to take a series of actions that eventually accomplish the user’s goal.

Imitation learning can give a model a starting point: how to click, how to navigate, what a reasonable workflow looks like. Reinforcement learning lets it learn from the consequences of those actions. If an action looks reasonable locally but leads to a dead end several steps later, the training signal can help the model favor a better approach.

That’s the connection to long-term planning. The model needs to connect the final outcome with decisions made earlier, while also checking whether its plan is working and adjusting when something unexpected happens. In an interactive environment, planning and execution have to work together.

But I wouldn’t say reinforcement learning automatically produces that ability. A lot depends on the tasks, the feedback, and whether training actually requires sustained sequences of decisions. I’m describing the general mechanism here, rather than making a claim about Operator’s specific training recipe.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning better sequential strategies, but does not characterize RL as eliciting a foundation model’s generalization ability on sufficiently complex tasks.

r002.rationale: It says imitation learning provides a starting point, but does not say RL elicits autonomous exploration.

r003.rationale: It links imitation learning’s starting point with RL learning from consequences, then describes checking whether a plan is working and adjusting when something unexpected happens, conveying learned self-correction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reinforcement learning plays an important role because long-term planning isn’t just about writing out a good plan. It’s about taking an action, observing what changed, and deciding what to do next. For an agent like Operator, the environment can behave differently from what it expected, so it needs to revise its plan and recover from mistakes.

Imitation learning can give the model a starting point by showing it successful behavior. Reinforcement learning can then help it learn which decisions actually lead to completing a task over many steps. The challenge is credit assignment: if a task succeeds or fails much later, which earlier actions deserve credit or blame?

So I would see reinforcement learning as a way to train planning through interaction and feedback. But I wouldn’t attribute all of Operator’s planning ability to it without knowing the training details. The underlying model, the observations it receives, and how the task is structured also matter.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning through interaction and feedback, but does not say reinforcement learning elicits a foundation model’s generalization on sufficiently complex tasks.

r002.rationale: It says imitation learning provides a starting point, but does not describe reinforcement learning eliciting autonomous exploration after demonstrations.

r003.rationale: The response mentions revising plans and recovering from mistakes, and says imitation learning provides a starting point. It does not clearly state that reinforcement learning elicits self-correction after simple demonstrations guide a foundation model.
